name: Pediatric anterolateral approach to the distal tibia
corridor: Between tibia and fibula in line with fourth metatarsal, through extensor retinaculum with anterior-compartment tendons retracted medially

positioning.text: Position supine on a radiolucent table with the ankle freely mobile and AP, lateral, mortise, and oblique imaging available.

setup.text: Use CT for displaced articular or transitional patterns, confirm swelling has resolved, and plan a physis-respecting reduction and fixation strategy.

surface_landmarks.text: Mark tibial crest, fibula, ankle joint, fourth-metatarsal axis, extensor tendons, and distal tibial physis.

incision.text: Center a straight incision over the fracture between tibia and fibula in line with the fourth metatarsal; tailor length to fragment, implant, and child size.

superficial_interval.text: Raise full-thickness flaps and open extensor retinaculum while protecting superficial sensory branches and extensor tendons.

deep_interval.text: Retract anterior-compartment tendons medially; mobilize peroneus tertius and anterior-compartment muscle only when proximal extension is necessary.

layers.text: Skin, full-thickness flap, extensor retinaculum, anterior-compartment tendon plane, periosteum/capsule, then distal tibial fragment.

structures_encountered.text: Extensor retinaculum, anterior-compartment tendons, peroneus tertius, distal tibial physis, capsule, and anterolateral fragment are encountered.

structures_at_risk.text: Superficial and deep peroneal nerves, anterior tibial vessels, extensor tendons, physis/perichondral ring, fragment periosteum, and articular cartilage are at risk.

danger_zones.text: Minimize periosteal stripping and avoid fixation trajectories that unnecessarily cross the open physis or penetrate joint.

retraction_hazards.text: Retract anterior tendons medially as a protected unit and avoid forceful pressure on deep neurovascular bundle or tenuous skin flaps.

exposure.text: Provides direct access to lateral distal-tibial and anterolateral articular fragments while preserving medial soft tissue.

limitations.text: Medial and posteromedial fragments are not directly visualized and proximal extension increases anterior-compartment dissection.

extensions.text: Extend only enough to mobilize anterior-compartment muscle proximally or add a separate fragment-specific medial/posterior window.

indications.text: Use for distal-tibial fractures extending laterally, particularly a smaller anterolateral fragment whose fracture exits laterally at articular surface.

relative_contraindications.text: Choose anteromedial exposure when a large anterolateral fragment extends toward medial malleolus or when lateral skin is compromised.

implant_implications.text: Use epiphyseal, metaphyseal, or transphyseal fixation only as dictated by skeletal maturity and pattern, minimizing physeal injury and ensuring extra-articular placement.

fluoroscopy_implications.text: Confirm anatomic joint reduction, physeal alignment, limb axis, and implant containment on AP, lateral, mortise, and oblique images.

closure.text: Restore retinaculum, confirm free tendon excursion, obtain hemostasis, and close soft tissue and skin separately without tension.

complications.text: Complications include physeal arrest, angular deformity, leg-length discrepancy, peroneal neuropathy, tendon adhesions, wound problems, infection, stiffness, and arthritis.

bailouts.text: Add a separate small fragment-directed incision when reduction cannot be verified without excessive periosteal or soft-tissue stripping.

procedure_applications.condition: A displaced lateral or anterolateral physeal/articular fragment requires direct reduction

questions.question: Which way are extensor tendons retracted?
What fracture morphology favors this approach?
questions.answer: A smaller anterolateral fragment with a lateral articular exit.

questions.question: What biologic structure must be preserved?
questions.answer: The periosteal and physeal blood supply.
